chapter_theme: A single song at Tirukkovalur (திருக்கோவலூர், கோவை மாநகர்): the poet asks whether he will cease to be caught by women's breasts, eyes, hair, lips and smiles, and praises the supreme lord whom the Vedas and the gods cannot see, in a town loud with Vedic chant and festival.

733.reading: The poet speaks of sinful, foolish women puffed with pride, their breasts like tender coconuts, eyes sharper than a spear, hair weighed with jewels, lips sweet as nectar and moon faces, and asks whether, so that his trouble ends, he will give up being drawn into that essence of infatuation. The praise names the supreme lord whom the four Vedas, Vishnu and Brahma cannot see, Murugan by the grace of the First, whose feet the gods all worship, the hero of the vel at Kovai, where the Vedas are chanted and festival and Agamic sounds roar, dwelling with the maid reared by the elephant.
733.nuance: The plea is short and set inside a long catalogue of the women's parts. கோதை யானையினோடு is Devayanai, named by her elephant nurture. கோவை is the shrine's name shortened.

links.note: 733 lists the women's eyes as sharper than a spear (பார்வையாமிகு கூரயில்) among the parts that draw the poet into infatuation, and asks to be freed of it. Naladiyar 44 refuses those who call eyes lilies, carp or spears (பொருகயல் வேலென்று) and sees the eye as a scooped palm fruit. The song keeps the poets' simile and prays against its pull; the Naladiyar dismantles the simile itself.
